    Track 4 · Advanced · Lesson 8

    Serving and inference optimization

    After this lesson you can explain what an inference server does, why the KV cache and continuous batching matter, the latency-vs-throughput trade-off, how big a KV cache gets, what chunked prefill, prefix caching and multi-LoRA serving buy you, and how serving choices connect to the quantization you learned in 4.6.

    Level: advanced Read time: ~13 min Prerequisites: Multi-task training and curriculum Updated: 13 Nov 2026

    You exported and deployed a model in Track 3. This lesson is what's happening inside that endpoint — and the knobs that decide whether it costs you a little or a lot to run.

    What an inference server does

    A naive loop calls model.generate() for one request at a time — fine for a demo, terrible for production. An inference server like vLLM sits in front of the model and turns it into an efficient, concurrent service: it batches requests, manages memory, and streams tokens back. BrewSLM's deploy targets a vLLM endpoint (among others).

    The KV cache: don't recompute the past

    Generation is autoregressive (Track 0): each new token attends to all previous tokens. Recomputing the attention keys and values for the whole prefix at every step would be quadratic waste. The KV cache stores those keys and values so each step only computes the new token's — the single biggest reason generation is tractable. Its cost is memory: the cache grows with sequence length and batch size, and managing it well is most of what a serving engine does. vLLM's PagedAttention (Kwon et al. 2023, arXiv 2309.06180) stores the cache in fixed-size blocks, like virtual-memory pages, so requests of different lengths don't waste memory on reserved-but-unused space.

    How big is the KV cache? Work it out

    Every layer stores one key and one value vector per KV head for every token:

    KV bytes per token = 2 (K and V) × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes per element
KV bytes total     = KV bytes per token × tokens in the cache (summed over all requests)

    Take the numbers from the model's config.json (head_dim = hidden_size ÷ num_attention_heads when the config doesn't list it):

    Model (config)Per token, 16-bitOne full-length request
    SmolLM2-135M: 30 layers, 3 KV heads, head_dim 642 × 30 × 3 × 64 × 2 B = 23,040 B ≈ 22.5 KiB8,192 tokens → 180 MiB
    Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: 28 layers, 2 KV heads, head_dim 1282 × 28 × 2 × 128 × 2 B = 28,672 B = 28 KiB32,768 tokens → 896 MiB

    Now serve Qwen2.5-1.5B to 64 users at once with 4,096-token conversations: 28 KiB × 4,096 × 64 = 7 GiB of KV cache, more than double the ~3 GB of bf16 weights. At scale the cache, not the model, decides how many requests fit. Three things shrink it: grouped-query attention (both models above share each K/V head across several query heads; with one KV head per query head, Qwen2.5-1.5B's cache would be 6× larger), an 8-bit KV cache (half the bytes; Lesson 4.6), and hybrid architectures that keep a full KV cache in only some layers (Qwen3.5-2B has 6 full-attention layers out of 24; the linear-attention layers keep a fixed-size state instead). For the training-side memory budget, see Lesson 1.15.

    Continuous batching: keep the GPU full

    Requests arrive at different times and finish at different lengths. Static batching waits for a whole batch, then runs it to completion — leaving the GPU idle as fast requests wait for slow ones. Continuous batching swaps finished sequences out and new ones in every step, keeping the GPU saturated. This is the main reason a good server delivers many times the throughput of a loop. The idea, scheduling per iteration rather than per request, comes from Orca (Yu et al., OSDI 2022).

    Prefill, decode, and chunked prefill

    Each request has two phases. Prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass and writes its KV cache; it is compute-heavy and sets the time to first token. Decode then produces one token per step; it reads all the weights and the cache for each token, so it is limited by memory bandwidth. A long prefill arriving mid-stream used to stall every running decode for its whole length. Chunked prefill (Agrawal et al. 2024, Sarathi-Serve, arXiv 2403.02310) splits long prompts into chunks and mixes them into decode steps under a per-step token budget. vLLM enables it by default where it can; its budget, max_num_batched_tokens, trades the two latencies: smaller values (e.g. 2,048) keep time per output token steady, larger ones get first tokens out sooner and raise throughput.

    Prefix caching: don't redo the same prompt

    Many requests start with the same text: a long system prompt, a tool list, a shared document, or the earlier turns of a chat. Prefix caching keeps the KV blocks of prompts already seen and reuses them when a new request starts with the same tokens, so that part of the prefill is skipped. vLLM's automatic prefix caching (enable_prefix_caching, on by default in current versions) matches by hashing KV blocks; llama.cpp's server reuses a slot's cache (--cache-prompt, on by default). It is a large win for tool routers (Lesson 4.12) and retrieval prompts, and does nothing for prompts that share no prefix or for long generations, since it only shortens prefill. To get the benefit, put the fixed parts of the prompt first and the per-request parts last.

    Many fine-tunes, one server: multi-LoRA

    If you trained several LoRA adapters on one base model (one per customer or task), you don't need one server per adapter. Multi-LoRA serving keeps one copy of the base weights in GPU memory and applies the right adapter per request, batching requests for different adapters together (S-LoRA, Sheng et al. 2023, arXiv 2311.03285). In vLLM:

    vllm serve HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M-Instruct \
  --enable-lora \
  --lora-modules router=./adapters/router support=./adapters/support \
  --max-loras 2 --max-lora-rank 16     # rank >= the largest adapter's rank
# each request picks an adapter by name: {"model": "router", ...}

    llama.cpp's server can load several adapters too (--lora with comma-separated files, scales set through its /lora-adapters endpoint). Adapters cost a little speed per request compared with a merged model, so merge (Track 3's export) when you serve only one.

    Latency vs throughput: the core trade

    • Latency — how long one request waits: time to first token (TTFT, mostly prefill), time per output token after that (TPOT, also called inter-token latency, ITL; mostly decode), and end-to-end time. What an interactive user feels.
    • Throughput — total tokens/second across all requests. What sets your cost per million tokens.

    They pull against each other: bigger batches raise throughput (cheaper) but can raise per-request latency. Tune to the use case — a chat UI optimizes latency; a nightly batch job optimizes throughput.

    # same model, two serving goals
chat UI (interactive)  ->  small batches, low latency      (fast first token)
batch job (offline)    ->  large batches, high throughput  (cheap per token)

# quantized weights (AWQ / GPTQ / FP8) use less memory
#   -> a bigger KV cache + larger batches fit -> often more throughput
#   (measure at your batch size: at large batch, int4 dequant can eat the gain)

    From 4.6

    Quantized serving compounds these wins: a 4-bit model (AWQ/GPTQ on GPU) uses less memory, which means a bigger KV cache and larger batches fit, and at batch 1 fewer bytes are read per token, which cuts latency. At large batch sizes weight-only int4 can become dequantization- or compute-bound and may not raise throughput, so measure at your batch size. Serving and compression are one decision.

    Key idea

    A serving engine like vLLM turns a model into a cheap, concurrent service via the KV cache (don't recompute the prefix; size it as 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes per token) and continuous batching (keep the GPU full), with chunked prefill, prefix caching and multi-LoRA on top. Tune the latency-vs-throughput trade to the use case, and remember quantization buys serving headroom, not just disk.

    Key terms

    inference server
    A service (e.g. vLLM) that batches, schedules, and streams generation efficiently.
    vLLM
    A high-throughput inference engine using paged attention for KV-cache management.
    KV cache
    Stored attention keys/values for prior tokens so each step only computes the new token's.
    continuous batching
    Swapping finished requests out and new ones in each step to keep the GPU saturated.
    latency vs throughput
    Per-request speed vs total tokens/second; bigger batches favor throughput over latency.
    PagedAttention
    vLLM's block-based KV-cache layout (arXiv 2309.06180) that avoids reserving memory a request may never use.
    prefill / decode
    Processing the prompt in one parallel pass (sets TTFT) vs generating one token per step (sets TPOT, bandwidth-bound).
    chunked prefill
    Splitting long prompts into chunks mixed with decode steps, so one long prompt doesn't stall everyone's next token.
    prefix caching
    Reusing the KV cache of a prompt prefix already seen (system prompt, tool list, chat history) to skip that part of prefill.
    multi-LoRA serving
    One base model in memory serving many LoRA adapters, chosen per request by name.
    quantized serving
    Serving a low-bit model so more KV cache / larger batches fit, raising throughput.
